A linguistic is defined here as the avoidance of certain words on certain occasions due to misfortune associated with those words. These circumstances depend on belief; they can be widespread or marginal. The avoidance of certain words may depend on the time of the day or action carried out. For instance, not only is sweeping not allowed when someone eats, but uttering the word tʃãã `broom' is also forbidden. Also, mentioning certain animal names is excluded as they may either be tabooed by someone present, due to his/her animal totem and/or its meat is forbidden, or attract the animal's attention, i.e. the belief that the animal may feel it is called out. The strategy is to substitute a word with another, often undertaking a metonymic strategy.

The second column of Table ( ) contains expressions called synonyms taboo synonyms; they are substitutes to the words of the the first column. The substitutes are usually complex stem nouns with a transparent descriptive meaning. Most of them use the stem tɪ́ɪ́ná `owner of', e.g. néŋ-tɪ̄ɪ̄nā , lit. arm|hand-owner.of, `elephant', the one with a big arm. The stem tɪ́ɪ́ná `owner of' can be characterized as a noun with an incomplete semantics which normally requires to be in an associative construction with another noun (i.e. person characterised by, owner of, or responsible for) and always appear following the `possessed’ stem. Mampruli daana , mai , and dhū seem to correspond to the meaning of Chakali tɪɪna .
summary: The passage defines a linguistic taboo as the avoidance of certain words in particular circumstances because of beliefs about misfortune, and notes that such avoidance can be tied to time, activities, or the presence of tabooed animals or their names. To replace these forbidden words, speakers use taboo synonyms, often transparent descriptive compounds built with the stem tɪ́ɪ́ná “owner of,” which functions as an incomplete semantic noun in associative constructions.

Compulsory prior to any communicative exchange, trigger both attention and respect. When meeting with elders, one should squat or bend forward hands-on-knees while greeting. Praise names can be used in greetings, e.g. ɪ́tʃà `respect to you and to your clan'. In Table , typical greeting lines with some responses are provided. Note that the forms for morning and afternoon greetings are also used by the Gonjas.

The second singular plural ma is added, i.e. ánsùmōō $ $ māānsùmōō , when there is more than one addressee or when there is a single person but the greetings are intended to the entire house/family: thus the number distinction ɪ / ma does not correspond to a politeness function. Chakali morning and afternoon resemble those of and other languages of the area. The response to various greetings such as ɪ́ dɪ́á `(how is) your house?', ʔánsà `welcome, thanks' and many others is the multifunctional expression ʔàwó , which is, among other things, a sign of appraisal of the interlocutor's concerns. The same expression is found in , but its function is believed to be slightly different. I was told that the more extensive the greetings, the more respect one shows the addressee. For instance, the elders do not appreciate the tendency of the youths to morning-greet as ã̄sūmō , but prefer something like áánsùùmōōō .

Other ritualized expressions often used are: tʃɔ̄pɪ̄sɪ́ ālɪ̀ɛ̀ lit. morning two, `long time no see' (Section ); bámùŋ kɔ́rɛ́ɪ́ lit. all.+hum extent (unknown origin), `how are all your people?', ànɪ́ mà wʊ̀zʊ́ʊ́rɪ́ tɪ̀ŋ , lit. and your day, used after any bad event which happened to someone, e.g. referring to a funeral day, when the speaker has not seen the addressee since that day, among other expressions.
summary:
Greeting rituals are compulsory before any communicative exchange and are meant to show both attention and respect; when greeting elders, one should squat or bend forward with hands on the knees. Greetings may include praise names, and longer greeting exchanges are considered more respectful; the plural addressee form *ma* is used when greeting multiple people or an entire household, but this number distinction is not a politeness marker.  

Responses to many greetings use the multifunctional expression *ʔàwó*, and several other ritualized expressions are also described, such as forms meaning “long time no see,” “how are all your people?”, and a phrase used after bad events.

An idiom is a composite expression which does not convey the literal meaning 
of the composition of its parts. Common among many African languages is a 
strategy by which abstract nominals are expressed in idiomatic compounds. 
These compounds are made of stems whose meanings are disassociated from their 
ordinary usage.

Some examples have already been provided in Section . In Chakali, words identifying mental states and habits/behaviors are often idiomatic, e.g. síínʊ̀màtɪ́ɪ́nà ( sii-nʊma-tɪɪna , lit. eye-hot-owner) `wild' or nʊ̃̀ã̀pʊ̀mmá ( nʊ̃ã-pʊmma , lit. mouth-white) `unreserved'. Even though the expression síínʊ̀màtɪ́ɪ́nà is made out of three lexical roots, it is a ``sealed'' expression and is associated with the manner in which a person behaves, i.e. a wild person. The sequence jaa nʊ̃ã dɪgɪmaŋa in ( ), lit. do-mouth-one, is also treated as an idiomatic expression.

3pl do mouth one help

Needless to say, it is often difficult to distinguish between an idiomatic
expression and an expression in which only one of the components is use in a
 non-literal sense.
summary: The passage explains that many African languages use idiomatic compounds to express abstract nominal meanings, with the component stems often losing their ordinary literal senses. In Chakali, words for mental states and habits are frequently formed this way, such as expressions meaning “wild” or “unreserved,” which are treated as fixed idioms even though they are built from several lexical roots. It also notes that it can be difficult to tell whether an expression is fully idiomatic or whether only one part is used non-literally.
